claims.text: High configurational entropy prevents phase segregation in near-equiatomic, multi-element solid-solution nanoparticles at temperatures up to approximately 1200 K.
High configurational entropy prevents nanoparticle coarsening at temperatures up to approximately 1200 K.
Suppressing segregation and coarsening preserves structural and chemical stability in catalytic and thermoelectric environments.
Large mixing entropy controls maintenance of a single-phase solid-solution structure with minimized phase boundaries.
High entropy reduces the free-energy difference between competing phases.
The entropy-related reduction in free-energy differences hinders phase separation or elemental clustering.
The proposed entropy mechanism slows nanoparticle coarsening at elevated temperatures.
Strictly near-equiatomic nanoparticles will exhibit less compositional segregation than off-equiatomic nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions.
Strictly near-equiatomic nanoparticles will retain a single-phase structure better than off-equiatomic nanoparticles under identical thermal conditions.
Off-equiatomic nanoparticles will show more pronounced secondary-phase formation than near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Mono- or binary metallic nanoparticles have lower configurational entropy than the proposed near-equiatomic multi-element nanoparticles.
Mono- or binary metallic nanoparticles will degrade more rapidly through phase changes or grain growth under comparable high-temperature conditions.
Entropy stabilization may fail above approximately 1200 K, permitting phase separation.
Strongly oxidizing environments may overcome entropy stabilization and produce additional oxide phases.
The stability threshold and magnitude of stabilization depend on the particular elemental combination and processing history.
Equivalent segregation or coarsening in near-equiatomic and off-equiatomic samples would falsify the claim that configurational entropy alone preserves stability.
